title: Man. Post. Cap. II: two formulations — miseries of life vs hereditary corruption; Placeus vs Garissoles
pass_a_gloss: Therefore with the name of penalty set aside, you could have instituted the question thus without any ambiguity: Why are we born liable to the miseries of this life, to the death of the body, and to eternal death? is it because the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us proximately and immediately? or because without such imputation, his viciousness has been derived from him into us, and transfused by natural propagation? You affirm the former, I the latter. Or thus: Why do we draw from Adam hereditary moral corruption, which is wont to be called original sin? Is it because by God the Judge the first actual sin of Adam is imputed to us, and for the penalty of that imputed sin, that it may be vindicated, and justice satisfied, that moral corruption is inflicted which is itself also sin, and the fountain of other sins? Or truly because, without such imputation, this is the law of nature constituted before the sin, that each thing generate its like, man a man, the corrupt the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? You again assert the former, I the latter. Although however the status of the question, thus proposed accommodatingly to your mind, is not utterly inconvenient, yet it does not yet satisfy me in every part: for it expresses rather the parts of the question, than the universal question itself.
pass_b_english: So drop the word penalty, and you could have put the question without ambiguity: Why are we born liable to the miseries of this life, to bodily death, and to eternal death? Because Adam's first actual sin is imputed to us proximately and immediately? Or because, without any such imputation, his viciousness has come down from him into us and been poured through by natural propagation? You affirm the first; I the second. Or put it this way: Why do we draw from Adam that hereditary moral corruption usually called original sin? Because God the Judge imputes Adam's first actual sin to us, and, as the penalty of that imputed sin—so that it may be avenged and justice satisfied—inflicts that moral corruption which is itself sin and the spring of other sins? Or rather because, without such imputation, this was nature's law before the fall: like begets like—man a man, the corrupt the corrupt, the vicious the vicious, the leprous the leprous? Again you assert the first; I the second. Though the state of the question, framed to fit your mind, is not wholly unserviceable, it still does not satisfy me on every side: it states the parts of the question more than the question as a whole.
source_text: Misso igitur poenae nomine, potuisses sic quaestionem instituisse sine ulla ambiguitate: Cur nascamur obnoxii miseriis hujus vitae, morti corporis, et morti aeternae? an quia nobis imputetur proxime et immediate primum peccatum actuale Adami? aut quia sine ejusmodi imputatione, vitiositas ejus ab eo in nos derivata est, et per propagationem naturalem transfusa? Tu prius affirmas, ego posterius. Vel sic, Cur trahimus ab Adamo corruptionem moralem haereditariam, quae peccatum originale dici solet? An quia nobis a Deo Judice primum peccatum actuale Adami imputetur, ac in ejus imputati poenam, ut vindicetur, et justitiae satisfiat, infligatur illa corruptio moralis, quae et ipsa peccatum est, et fons aliorum peccatorum? Aut vero quia, sine ejusmodi imputatione, haec est naturae lex ante peccatum constituta, ut sui quaeque res similem gignat, homo hominem, corruptus corruptum, vitiosus vitiosum, leprosus leprosum? Tu rursus prius asseris, ego posterius. Quamvis autem status questionis, ita propositus accommodate ad mentem tuam, non prorsus incommodus sit, nondum tamen mihi omni ex parte satisfacit: exprimit enim potius partes questionis, quam ipsam quaestionem universam.

lemmas.gloss: setting aside the name of penalty

choices.choice: Placeus: miseries/corruption by propagation, not immediate actual-sin imputation
